title: One Newton step on a small system
narration: Newton's method updates the current point x c like this: x plus equals x c minus the inverse Jacobian times F at x c. Let's try it on a tiny system. F has two parts: x one squared minus four, and x two squared minus sixteen. Our current point is x one equals four and x two equals eight. [[a]]First we evaluate F there. That gives twelve and forty eight. [[b]]Next comes the Jacobian, the matrix of derivatives. Here it is diagonal, with two times x one, which is eight, and two times x two, which is sixteen. [[c]]In practice we never form the inverse. Instead we solve the linear system J times s equals minus F. [[d]]Dividing minus twelve by eight gives minus one point five, and minus forty eight by sixteen gives minus three. That is the Newton step s. [[e]]Finally we add the step to the current point: four minus one point five is two point five, and eight minus three is five. That is x plus. The solution is two and four, so we are getting closer. The paper's trick is to do this linear solve cheaply, in low precision.
